filename: WLLS, liver health, doctors note, PDSRG, clinical note
question_original: Would someone diagnosed with liver disease benefit from taking Dotfits Weight Loss & Liver Support?
question_canonical: Would someone diagnosed with liver disease benefit from taking dotFIT Weight Loss & Liver Support?
answer:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

Thanks for contacting us. We do not promote any of our products as clinical solutions (i.e., to treat a medical condition). The goals of our health products are related to protection (i.e., before the fact). That said, because your client has an existing liver condition, any supplement they may use should be approved by their doctor. As an example, the green tea extract in Weight Loss & Liver Support (WLLS), which is EGCG, may be contraindicated in existing liver disease, but may help protect against it before the fact. To err on the side of caution, don’t recommend it without the doctor’s approval. You can give the doctor this link to the Practitioner Dietary Supplement Reference Guide (PDSRG), which is used for training and certification purposes only (not consumer-facing), and click on WeightLoss&LiverSupport to get the peer-reviewed science related to WLLS.

Thanks again and have a great night!

From the PDSRG

Safety

Adverse events, precautions, or contraindications with any ingredients in WLLS are rare or unknown in the general population when supplementing the diet properly, as described above. The section below is a high-level summary related to specific subpopulations. Qualified practitioners needing more information related to these categories, including drug interactions, are referred to the TRC Natural Medicine Data Base (TRCNMD), which is continually updated with emerging evidence-based data.

Precautions

Weight Loss & Liver Support (WLLS) is historically (a combination of ingredients has 13 years of widespread use) and generally considered a safe fat-loss aid. Theoretically, concomitant use of choline (much higher doses than found in this product) and atropine may decrease the effects and side effects of atropine.

Diabetes: Milk thistle constituents might lower blood glucose in patients with type 2 diabetes. People with diabetes using milk thistle products should closely monitor blood glucose levels. Dose adjustments to diabetes medications might be necessary. People with liver disorders should consult their physician before using a product containing EGCG. No IG studies reported more adverse events than the placebo groups. Much higher doses than contained in WLLS of NAC (i.e., a clinical need) should require a separate prescription from a qualified physician.

Contraindications (also see Precautions)

Weight Loss & Liver Support is contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation because of a lack of data for this population.

Because of NAC, do not take if using anticoagulant drugs or nitroglycerin.

Clinical research shows that milk thistle extract, alone or with tree turmeric extract, can lower blood glucose levels and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in patients with type 2 diabetes, including those already taking antidiabetes drugs. TAMOXIFEN (Nolvadex): theoretically, the milk thistle constituent silibinin might increase tamoxifen levels and interfere with its conversion to an active metabolite. However, this has not been shown in humans.

Adverse Reactions

Milk Thistle: Orally, milk thistle is usually well tolerated and considered safe when used orally and appropriately. A specific milk thistle extract standardized to contain 70% to 80% silymarin has been safely used in doses up to 420 mg daily for up to 4 years. Uncommon events may include an occasional laxative effect, nausea, diarrhea, dyspepsia, flatulence, abdominal bloating, fullness, or pain.

EGCG: Typical doses range from one to 10 cups of green tea daily without any adverse events. A very high intake of green tea may cause nausea, abdominal bloating, pain, flatulence, and diarrhea. It can also cause central nervous system stimulation and adverse effects such as dizziness, insomnia, fatigue, agitation, tremors, restlessness, and confusion. These effects are more common with higher doses of green tea or green tea extract, equivalent to 5–6 liters of tea per day. There have been reports of potential liver toxicity with regular ingestion of high-dose green tea extracts. To address these accounts, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) prepared an 89-page report concluding: “Based on the available data on the potential adverse effects of green tea catechins on the liver, the Panel concluded that there is evidence from interventional clinical trials that intake of doses equal to or above 800 mg EGCG/day taken as a food supplement statistically significantly increases serum transaminases in treated subjects compared to control.” The EFSA also stated, “From the clinical studies reviewed, there is no evidence of hepatotoxicity below 800 mg EGCG/day up to 12 months.” WLLS total dosage (3 tablets/day) contains the known safe and in-range effective dose of 600 mg of green tea (Camellia sinensis) leaf extract standardized to 98% polyphenols (588 mg), 80% catechins (480 mg), 45% EGCG (270 mg), and 2% caffeine (naturally occurring, 4 mg), which is well below the EGCG/GT upper limit described by the EFSA. Anyone with liver disorders should consult their doctor before considering EGCG use at any dosage. The dotFIT dosage and product duration recommendation would be considered safe and effective for the general population, including the overweight adult population.

Choline is not likely to cause side effects at doses up to 3,000 mg/day. Amounts at very high levels (over 9 g daily) can include sweating, a fishy body odor, and gastrointestinal distress.

Irvingia gabonensis: The only side effects reported using the specific standardized extract of Irvingia gabonensis (IGOB131) were flatulence, headaches, and difficulty sleeping, which were similar to the reports in the placebo group.

Upper Limit/Toxicity

Choline: The IOM set the UL for choline at 3,500 mg/day, and the LOAEL is 7,500 mg/day.

NAC: The LD50 for NAC in mice is 7,888 mg/kg, and in rats is 6,000 mg/kg. An Ames test performed on NAC was negative for mutagenicity.

Milk Thistle: There is no established UL and it is considered relatively safe for long-term use as directed.

EGCG: High doses of green tea or green tea extract, equivalent to 21–25 cups of tea per day, can cause gastrointestinal distress. The EFSA stated, “From the clinical studies reviewed, there is no evidence of hepatotoxicity below 800 mg EGCG/day up to 12 months.”

Irvingia gabonensis: There is no established UL or known toxicity data available at this time.

source_file: 2024/Weight-fat Loss Instructions.docx
filename: Weight-fat Loss Instructions
answer:
Goal setting, monitoring, and adjustments

Weight/Fat Loss

Use your dotFIT programs to get your true starting calories. All will be contained in your program, including necessary weekly adjustments, but below is a summary. If measuring body fat, measurements and adjustments are bi-weekly.

Weekly goal: lose 1–2 lbs/week or approximately 1% body fat every 2 weeks. Your target daily calories are slightly lower than your daily burn. This allows you to lose at least 1 lb per week without compromising performance gains. The more overweight, the greater the allowed weekly loss, with 2 lbs loss being the maximum when performance is part of the goal.

Monitoring: weigh/measure weekly in the same dress, at the same time, and on the same scale. If necessary (see below), only adjust calories in or out every 7 days.

Adjustments: a measurable or visual reduction in body fat and/or weight should take place in a fairly consistent manner, such as a decrease in circumference inches and/or the desired average decrease in weight or body fat per week. If progress stops or slows dramatically, one or a mixture of the following adjustments is all that will be necessary to restart the process:

- Increase daily activities (e.g., daily steps or other non-athletic/exercise activities).
- Standing and pacing burns 2–3 times more calories than sitting for the same time period.
- There are approximately 2,000–2,500 steps (depending on stride) in a mile. Walking 2,000 steps will burn approximately 75–150 more calories (depending on individual size) than sitting for the same time and only takes approximately 20–30 minutes and can be done anywhere, even in the office.
- Increase workout (generally aerobic-type) time or intensity, including adding interval cardio training.
- Decrease food intake approximately 200–300 calories/day or remove a small portion of your largest meal, and repeat this reduction if after 1 week there is no change in weight/body composition.
- Repeat the process any time weight or body fat is stable for at least one week.

Always remember: if you stop losing weight/fat, you only need to eat less, move more, or a combination of the two, regardless of what you read or hear from others.

When you have achieved your body composition goals, increase your calories to maintain desired weight.

Diet Monitoring & Adjustments for Body Fat Reduction

Program Algorithms

Adjustments:

Measurable or visual reduction in body fat and/or weight proceeds in a consistent manner, e.g., a decrease in circumference inches, and/or the desired average decrease in body fat per week.

If progress stops or slows dramatically, use one or a combination of adjustments to restart the process:

- Increase daily activities (e.g., daily steps or other non-athletic/exercise activities).
- Standing and pacing burns 1.5–2 times more calories than sitting for the same period.

- Increase cardio workout time and/or intensity and include interval training if necessary.
- Example: If doing 30 minutes 5 days/week, go to 45 minutes and add interval work within the time frame.
- Decrease food intake approximately 200 to 300 calories per day or remove a small portion (carbs/fats) of the largest meal other than the pre-workout meal (incorporate 3-days low/1-high as necessary).
- Add dietary support beyond baseline as necessary (thermogenic, energy partitioning, appetite control, etc.).

Repeat the process any time body fat is stable for at least one week. Always remember, if you are supplementing properly and you stop losing fat, you need to eat less, move/burn more, or use a combination of the two, regardless of what you read or hear from others. As you lower calorie intake, make sure your protein intake stays at or above 1 gm per pound of body weight to protect LBM.

In a powdered product, there is empty space between the top of the powder and the bottom of the lid. The actual term is called “slack-fill,” and its definition is: “Slack-fill is the difference between the actual capacity of a container and the volume of product contained therein.”

Since our powdered products are being filled by machines and not by hand, they can only fill to a certain height to avoid overfill and also include a scoop. With this, there will be this space between the top of the powder and the bottom of the lid. However, powder naturally decreases in volume with time and transport.

An easier-to-understand example that most people see in real life is a box of corn flakes that has 12 ounces of corn flakes. It could have between 1–3 inches of empty space at the top of the bag, inside the box. The corn flakes have settled, and it may look like you are getting less, but you are still getting 12 ounces of corn flakes.

Seems that this would be obvious, but more people are feeling that they are getting ripped off as a result of shrinkflation, so steps are being taken to make this “difference” more clear to consumers.

To help explain this, going forward, all powdered products will have this “slack-fill” image and statement:

question_original: One of our members asked why the Superblend does not have a 15:2 ratio of Zinc to copper. He says with the amount of zinc in the superblend it will remove all the copper from our body. Is this true?
question_canonical: Does the Alln1 SuperBlend's zinc content remove copper from the body, and why is its zinc-to-copper ratio not 15:2?
answer:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

Thanks for contacting us. The good news is that your member is not an expert, so no one should listen to him on this topic. First of all, many people don’t supplement anything and they are not copper deficient—meaning there is no way the body figures out how to make it automatically 15:2. The body uses what you give it and balances its needs based on levels (the triage factor). The goal is to have all the body can use by supplementing what we know the body doesn’t get from food. That’s what the Alln1 SuperBlendTM and our pill products do perfectly. Refer your member to the PDSRG Vitamin sections (see below). Ironically (and because we want it this way because of normal food intake), the zinc-to-copper ratio in the Alln1 SuperBlendTM is about 15:2—12 mg (12,000 µg) zinc; copper is 800 µg (0.8 gm). Therefore, 12,000:800 is approximately 15:2.

No amount of zinc below the RDA will remove the body’s copper.

Thanks again, and have a great weekend.

The daily amounts of vitamins and minerals currently known as the safe and optimal range are captured in the Practitioner’s Dietary Supplement Reference Guide (PDSRG) and contained within those documented amounts in the dotFIT formulas—the design of the Multivitamin and Mineral Formula (MVM).

source_file: 2024/liposomal creatine - full answer and ISSN slide.docx
filename: liposomal creatine - full answer and ISSN slide
answer:
The quick answer is that the 1000s of studies that prove creatine delivers on claims of safety and efficacy all use creatine monohydrate without a delivery system such as liposomes*. Everyone is trying to find a different complex that might work as well as just the creatine monohydrate, so that less creatine is needed to get the same (or better) results, thus gaining a marketing advantage. It has not happened yet (see below from the ISSN), as there are no human studies showing an advantage with a liposomal creatine. The good news is that creatine liposomal (or liposomal creatine) is still creatine monohydrate, so it doesn’t hurt. But the question is, does the liposome addition (fat delivery system) allow a better or lesser result? The only way to know would be to perform at least 50 different clinical trials versus creatine monohydrate alone, and let the winner prevail. However, there is probably no point, since we know creatine monohydrate works optimally at a determined dosage by body weight, and more doesn’t alter the outcome, so how does getting more to the target tissue matter? That said, it would be great if instead of using .045 gms/lb of body weight of creatine monohydrate as a maintenance dose to maximize skeletal muscle (and brain) stores, you could accomplish the same result with less, thus potentially saving money, if the theoretical formula is less expensive.

And yes, you should always take your creatine supplementation with food or a shake to maximize skeletal muscle uptake.

*Liposomal refers to a drug preparation that uses tiny, fat-like particles to deliver an active drug to the body.

4-Teaching Anchors

First law of thermodynamics: eliminates any basic alternate reasons for a plateau, specifically spontaneous energy storage, while answering all questions about why someone loses body fat no matter what method is used (other than surgery). This constitutes the bottom line in the energy change in any system and ties to all other anchors.

Societies' increasing fat storage is due to a lack of energy expenditure compared to energy intake (eating too much and moving too little). This severely restricts the macronutrient-related arguments, as well as fad diets being a general solution.

We are not prisoners of our genes. People do lose weight and keep it off. There is probably a set point range for most individuals that may be set by genetics. Where you end up on the range is determined by lifestyle (physical activity, eating habits, etc.). These genes control appetite, satiety, basal and exercise metabolism, and the point at which excess energy intake is converted to lean tissue or body fat. Ultimately, we can control energy in and out. In the final analysis, this eliminates the genetic argument while still admitting that there is an increased difficulty for some because of genetic inheritance.

Fat loss is not limited like hypertrophy. This eliminates the argument that one cannot lose any more weight or fat. We can always alter mass or composition by manipulating energy intake and expenditure (it is a matter of what one is willing or must do to get there). Additionally, this fact eliminates the “point of diminishing returns” excuse for a plateau.

answer:

Sucralose and cellulose (also see section in WheySmooth—page 29—and I pasted it below).

Partial answer to a question from a confused consumer who said sucralose was harmful:

Of course, there is nothing harmful about sucralose in proper amounts, or we would not use it, like anything else. In fact, sucralose is one of the seven FDA-approved non-nutritional sweeteners (also no calories). That said, because of expanding media, there will always be confusion and financial bias around any ingredient/food product, and therefore, we make an unflavored/unsweetened creatine and other all-natural sweetened or unflavored alternatives, such as protein powders, Alln1 SuperBlend™, etc., for people’s personal preferences. Mindful, as you probably know, we are an evidence-based R&D company for fitness programming and products. Meaning, our products are Practitioner Products sold through professional channels, not available in the mass market. And why we are the largest provider of 3rd-party-tested nutrition programs and products in the sport and fitness channels, including collegiate and professional sports. As we always like to say here in the scientific community, “while we are bound to the evidence-based facts, everyone else is entitled to their own opinion,” and that is why we have the natural alternatives. A reminder, as you probably know, natural can be very harmful to many people (think peanuts, fruits, shellfish, gluten, etc.—see attached slide), which is why natural foods have warning labels. We have more adverse reactions to monk fruit and stevia (natural allergies), which are in our all-natural products, than any other product we sell. We have none in the other powders.

FAQ:
Q: Why artificial sweeteners? Not included in All Natural WheySmooth or BestPlantProtein
A: Better and healthier than added sugar and FDA-approved (Ref. Sweetener docs here.) 4, 2022 meta, ref4
Added sugars are a leading cause of disease, and this is why the government warns and sets limits. Ref2
Better taste = continued use to improve fitness results—no downside in “normal health” users
Higher nutrition per calorie/sweetness to support desired body composition
Sucralose tested best of sweeteners and sucrose in weight management. Ref
Supports blood sugar (approved for diabetics)
Decreases risk of adverse reactions common with “natural” sweeteners (honey, stevia, lactose, fruit sugar residues, etc.) 27, 28
Supports weight control versus contributor. 2, 2022 meta, and CV health
Approved for children. 1

*The FDA established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) for sucralose of 5 milligrams per kilogram (Europe is 7 and Canada 11 mg/kg) of body weight (mg/kg per day). The ADI represents an amount 100 times less than the quantity of sucralose found to be safe in research studies. For a person weighing 150 pounds (68 kg), the US ADI equates to 340 mg of sucralose—the amount found in nine cans of diet soda or more than 28 individual packets of sucralose—consumed, on average, every day over a lifetime.

1. Policy Statement from the American Academy of Pediatrics. The Use of Nonnutritive Sweeteners in Children. Pediatrics, Volume 144, number 5, November 2019: e20192765.
2. Higgins et al. A randomized controlled trial contrasting the effects of 4 low-calorie sweeteners and sucrose on body weight in adults with overweight or obesity. Am J Clin Nutr 2019;109:1288–1301.

FYI: Because of its safety, EFSA decided to expand the sweetener’s use in foods for special medical purposes for children.

Sucralose

Sucralose is also an NNS and is made from sucrose by a process that substitutes three chloride atoms for three hydroxyl groups on the sucrose molecule. Sucralose is a very versatile NNS that is 450–650 times sweeter than sucrose, possesses a pleasant sweet taste, and has a quality and time-intensity profile that is close to that of sucrose, making it a popular NNS. Sucralose has been extensively studied, with more than 110 safety studies reviewed by the FDA in approving the use of sucralose as a general-purpose sweetener for food. A primary advantage of sucralose for consumers is its exceptional stability. It retains its sweetness over a wide range of temperature and storage conditions and in solutions over time. This stability allows manufacturers to create better-tasting foods and beverages and maintain the fresh flavor. Like Ace-K, sucralose is heat-stable, meaning that it stays sweet even when used at high temperatures during baking, making it a common sugar substitute in baked goods.

The FDA established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) for sucralose of 5 milligrams per kilogram (Europe’s is 7 mg/kg and Canada’s is 11 mg/kg) of body weight (mg/kg per day).* The amount of sucralose per serving in WheySmooth is ~34 mg.

*Out of safety precautions to protect all subgroups of people, the ADI represents an amount 100 times less than the quantity of sucralose found to be safe in research studies. For a person weighing 150 pounds (68 kg), the US ADI equates to 340 mg of sucralose—the amount found in nine cans of diet soda or more than 28 individual packets of sucralose—consumed, on average, every day over a lifetime.

Carboxymethyl Cellulose

Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), or cellulose gum, is a popular non-toxic cellulose (fiber) derivative, an FDA-approved food additive, and on the generally recognized as safe list (GRAS). CMC is used in food as a viscosity modifier or thickener and to stabilize emulsions (emulsifier) in food products. CMC is used extensively in gluten-free and reduced-fat food products such as WheySmooth. Use of CMC also ensures smooth dispersion in flavor oils and improves texture and overall quality.

Thanks again and good luck on your fitness journey. We will be with you all the way!

Spot reducing note

Losing body fat anywhere on the body requires consuming fewer calories than you burn, regardless of the type of diet you consume. The goal is to find a diet that you’re comfortable with so you can stick with it until you reach your goal, knowing there is no such thing as “spot reducing”—i.e., fat leaves the body from wherever it’s genetically programmed to lose it, and sometimes the places you want it to leave from first do not happen until later—but it will happen if you stay in the calorie deficit. You do this by eating less, moving more, or a combination of the two until you reach the goal. While aging can alter where you lose and store fat because of hormone shifts, the formula for losing body fat anywhere on the body is the same, including eventually leaving from any place first, second, or third.

Building or Maintaining Muscle While Losing Body Fat and the dotFIT Program

Building or maintaining muscle while losing body fat, depending on age and training experience (younger and less experience make the gains easier and faster), is not often easy to accomplish because the formula requires a few components that you need to adhere to: 1) a daily menu plan that has the correct calories and foods, including protein quantity matched to the body composition goal; 2) a dietary supplement program to feed muscle while starving fat—i.e., deliver high nutrition with little to no calories—meaning you will need at least a multivitamin and mineral (MVM) and extra protein to help recover and maintain structural and functional integrity (when calories are limited to reduce body fat, you also limit the nutrients that would otherwise be contained in those calories); 3) regular unaccustomed resistance exercise. source_file: 2025/Bio-engineered food - GMO.docx
filename: Bio-engineered food - GMO
answer:
What Are Bioengineered Ingredients?

Bioengineered (BE) ingredients are ingredients in food that come from plants, animals, or microorganisms whose DNA has been altered through modern biotechnology (genetic engineering).

In simple terms:
Bioengineered ingredients = ingredients made from genetically modified organisms (GMOs).

This definition is used legally in the U.S. National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard (NBFDS), which requires BE foods to be labeled.

✔️ Simple Definition for Consumers
Bioengineered ingredients are GMO-derived ingredients that still contain detectable genetically modified DNA or protein and therefore must be labeled under U.S. law.

📌 Key Points
1. BE Ingredients Contain Detectable Modified Genetic Material
To be labeled “bioengineered,” the ingredient must contain detectable GMO DNA or proteins.

If the GM DNA is removed or destroyed during processing (common with oils, sugars, starches), the product may NOT be labeled BE—even if the crop was genetically modified.

2. BE = GMO (legally, same category), but not all GMOs must be labeled

Examples of GM crops used in BE ingredients:
Corn
Soybeans
Canola
Sugar beets
Cottonseed
Papaya (Hawaiian)
Certain potatoes
Certain apples
Squash

Examples of Common Bioengineered Ingredients

These come from genetically modified crops and often remain BE after processing:

From Corn
High-fructose corn syrup
Corn starch (sometimes)
Corn flour (if not extensively processed)

From Soy
Soy protein concentrate/isolate
Soy lecithin (sometimes BE, sometimes not)
Soy oil (not labeled BE because the DNA is removed)

From Canola
Canola oil (usually not BE-labeled—DNA removed)

From Sugar Beets
Table sugar (often not BE-labeled because no DNA remains)

From Cottonseed
Cottonseed oil

From Potatoes/Apples
Certain varieties engineered to resist browning or bruising

What Foods Commonly Contain BE Ingredients?
Packaged snacks
Sweetened beverages
Breakfast cereals
Baking mixes
Protein bars
Frozen meals
Condiments
Many ultra-processed foods

What Foods Are Usually Free From Bioengineered Ingredients?
Organic products (by law, organic cannot contain GMOs)
Whole, fresh animal products (meat, eggs, dairy)
Whole fruits and vegetables (except a few GM varieties)

Why Are BE Ingredients Used?
Companies use bioengineered crops because they offer:
Higher yields
Pest resistance
Herbicide tolerance
Reduced food waste (e.g., non-browning apples)
Cost savings in large-scale food production

⚖️ Labeling Rules (U.S.)
Foods must disclose BE status if:
They contain detectable modified DNA
Their ingredients are on the USDA’s BE list

Allowed forms of disclosure:
The word “bioengineered”
A symbol
Electronic/digital link (QR code)

✔️ Simple Definition for Consumers
Bioengineered ingredients are GMO-derived ingredients that still contain detectable genetically modified DNA or protein and therefore must be labeled under U.S. law.

Thanks for contacting us. Fueling bodybuilding workouts adequately with carbohydrates (CHO) is unique to your training phase—i.e., off-season (bulking/pure muscle gain focus) or in-season (preparing for competition). source_file: 2025/Caffeine vasodialator notes.docx
filename: Caffeine vasodialator notes
answer:
Coffee Effects

The alkaloid caffeine contained in coffee has positive inotropic and chronotropic effects on the heart via catecholamine release and raises systolic blood pressure; for instance, 250 mg raises systolic pressure by 10 mm Hg after 15 minutes. Caffeine causes mild cerebral vasoconstriction, relaxes bronchial smooth muscles, increases gastric acid secretion via gastrin release, and transiently increases diuresis. Theobromine and theophylline alkaloids in caffeine act as vasodilators, cough suppressants, and bronchodilators. The habituation effect occurs over time.

Four to five cups of coffee daily can reduce gout attacks in men by up to 40% through increased uric acid excretion, while more than six cups may reduce attacks by 59%, although decaffeinated coffee is preferable as a supportive measure.

Coffee enriched with chlorogenic acid–rich green coffee bean extracts showed increased DNA protection against oxidative damage and increased plasma-reduced glutathione via glutathione reductase activation. Roasting lowers chlorogenic acid, trigonelline, cafestol, and kahweol levels while increasing melanoidin and nicotinic acid levels.

Coffee and healthy aging

The researchers found a correlation between how much caffeine the women typically drank (which was mostly from coffee) when they were between 45 and 60 years old and their likelihood of healthy aging. After adjusting for other factors that could affect aging, such as their overall diet, how much they exercised and whether they smoked, those who consumed the most caffeine (equivalent to nearly seven eight-ounce cups of coffee per day) had odds of healthy aging that were 13 percent higher than those who consumed the least caffeine (equivalent to less than one cup per day).

Drinking tea or decaffeinated coffee was not associated with healthy aging, the researchers found. That may be because the study participants generally consumed less tea and decaffeinated coffee overall, so perhaps there were fewer chances for the researchers to find benefits linked to them, said [NAME], an adjunct professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto who led the study. Tea and decaf coffee also have less caffeine, and tea has different plant compounds from regular coffee, so that may explain the results, too, she added.

Despite the benefits shown for food intake, satiety and body composition, the mechanism by which CFE exerts its benefits largely remains unknown. It was therefore an aim of this study to investigate possible biochemical mechanisms of CFE. Following 16-weeks of supplementation and despite the reduction in calorie intake in the CFE group, there were no associated changes in satiety hormone markers (namely leptin and ghrelin) from baseline in the CFE group. The placebo group however showed significantly elevated levels of leptin, cortisol and NPY from baseline. Typically, when leptin levels increase, satiety would improve, and weight loss or maintenance occur. However, as leptin is produced in adipose tissue25, as fat mass increases, leptin production increases26,27. Weight gain is also associated with a decreased sensitivity to leptin27, reducing the ability to achieve satiety. Leptin acts to reduce the desire to eat28, while cortisol29 and NPY28 increases the desire to eat. Therefore, at times of hunger, leptin levels are typically low and NPY levels high, initiating a feeding desire and increasing cortisol levels. The elevated cortisol leads to eating, which in turn increases leptin levels, reducing NPY activation and subsequent cortisol levels30,31.

Cortisol can induce a dose-dependent increase in leptin32, and this may be why leptin and cortisol have been shown to have inverse circadian rhythms, indicating a possible satiety regulatory relationship33,34.

This theory is partially supported by the correlation data (Table 3), where it is shown that in the placebo group, as leptin values increase so does the fat mass, while cortisol levels decrease (inverse relationship with leptin). An effect not seen in the CFE group. This is also supported by a study where CFE was shown to reduce anxiety and stress as well as act on cortisol regulation35.

source_file: 2025/Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate folate forms best for supps.docx
filename: Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate folate forms best for supps
answer:
No, they are not exactly the same; Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate is a form of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate that is stabilized by being a calcium salt. 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) is the biologically active form of folate (Vitamin B9) that the body can use directly, while Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate is the common, stable, and commercially available form of that active nutrient used in supplements.

Here's a breakdown:

5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF):

This is the naturally occurring, metabolically active form of folate found in the human circulation and in food. It's the form the body uses to convert homocysteine to methionine, among other vital functions.

Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate:

This is a synthetic, stable salt form of the active 5-MTHF. Adding calcium makes the naturally occurring 5-MTHF more stable and suitable for use in dietary supplements and food fortification.

In summary:

When you see "5-MTHF," "L-5-MTHF," or "Calcium L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate" on a supplement label, it refers to the same biologically active nutrient. The "calcium" part simply indicates the form it's formulated in for stability and availability in a supplement.

source_file: 2025/Carbs at night versus day time.docx
filename: Carbs at night versus day time
answer:
I did a literature search and didn’t find a definitive “recent” (2023–2025) study that unequivocally shows that consuming most carbohydrates at night is better than in the morning in all respects. The evidence is mixed, context-dependent, and often nuanced. However, I found a couple of interesting studies that suggest potential advantages (or at least no disadvantage) under certain conditions. Below is a summary and caveats.

Key Study of Interest

“Impact of carbohydrate timing on glucose metabolism and metabolic flexibility” ([NAME] et al., 2025)

This study compared post-exercise carbohydrate ingestion in the evening versus pre-exercise ingestion and no carbohydrate (control) in healthy, trained individuals. PubMed

The authors found that although morning glucose tolerance was reduced when carbohydrate was ingested the previous evening (after evening exercise), the metabolic flexibility (MetF)—i.e., ability to switch between fat and carbohydrate oxidation—was improved. PubMed

In particular, during an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), during the first hour after post-exercise carbohydrate intake, carbohydrate oxidation was 70–91% higher relative to control/pre-exercise ingestion. PubMed

The authors interpret this as suggesting that strategic evening carbohydrate intake (post-exercise) may help enhance metabolic flexibility, which in turn could support performance in subsequent training sessions. PubMed

While this doesn’t prove that “having most of your carbs at night is superior,” it does challenge the notion that evening carbohydrate intake is inherently detrimental. It suggests that in certain protocols—especially around training—late-day carbs might confer benefits in metabolic responsiveness.

Supporting & Contrasting Evidence

A recent review of carbohydrate supplementation strategies notes that timing, dose, and type of carbohydrate (and the gastrointestinal adaptation to repeated intake) matter a lot for performance and tolerance. MDPI

Another study, “Effects of Short-Term Nighttime Carbohydrate Restriction” ([NAME] et al., 2024), used a restriction of carbs after 4 p.m. (i.e., limiting evening carbs) and found improved fat metabolism and VO₂peak in a short-term training model. MDPI+1. But that’s a different angle (limiting evening carbs) rather than promoting them.

More broadly, studies of meal-timing and chrononutrition show that circadian alignment affects glucose tolerance and metabolic responses, which is often used as a caution against heavy late-night carb loads. Wikipedia+1

Some recent work also shows that high-glycemic carbohydrate meals may shorten sleep onset latency (i.e., help you fall asleep faster) when consumed in the evening, though that speaks more to sleep than metabolism per se. ScienceDirect

Interpretation & Practical Take-Home

The [NAME] et al. (2025) study is perhaps the closest to what you asked: it indicates that post-evening exercise carbohydrate consumption doesn’t necessarily impair, and may in fact enhance, metabolic flexibility and carbohydrate oxidation during subsequent tests.

However, there’s a trade-off: their data also showed poorer morning glucose tolerance under some conditions when carbs were consumed after evening exercise. PubMed

So it’s not a blanket endorsement of “all carbs at night” but rather suggests that strategic timing of evening carbs, especially in relation to training and when total daily macros are controlled, might be beneficial or at least safe.

If you like, I can dig further to find an even more recent (2023–2025) randomized trial where evening carbohydrate intake outperformed morning intake for body composition or performance. Do you want me to keep digging?

Studies that favor evening carbs (context-dependent)

Post-evening exercise carbs may enhance next-day metabolic flexibility.

A 2025 randomized, crossover study in trained adults compared carb intake after evening exercise vs. before exercise and vs. no carbs. Evening carbs impaired morning glucose tolerance but improved metabolic flexibility and carbohydrate oxidation during the subsequent OGTT—suggesting potential advantages for athletes who prioritize next-session performance and substrate switching. Taylor & Francis Online+3PMC+3PubMed+3

Concentrating carbs at dinner improved weight loss and satiety hormones in obesity.

A 6-month randomized trial in 78 obese police officers found that eating most carbs at dinner (within a hypocaloric diet) led to greater weight, waist, and body-fat reductions, lower hunger scores, and better glucose/insulin, lipids, and inflammatory markers than distributing carbs across the day. A follow-up paper from the same trial showed favorable shifts in leptin/ghrelin/adiponectin profiles with the dinner-carb pattern. PubMed+1

source_file: 2025/Cardio after weight training best -.docx
filename: Cardio after weight training best -
answer:
https://studyfinds.org/cardio-before-or-after-weights/?utm_source=studyfinds.beehiiv.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=studyfinds-newsletter-6-15-25

But the real differences emerged when it came to fat loss and muscle performance. Participants who lifted weights first experienced significantly greater reductions in overall body fat and visceral fat—the type of fat most strongly linked to cardiovascular disease risk.

Resistance training depletes muscle glycogen stores—the sugar that’s stored in the muscles, which acts as your body’s quick-access fuel. Imagine glycogen as petrol in your car’s fuel tank. When you lift weights first, you effectively drain this fuel tank, forcing your body to switch energy sources.

With glycogen stores already low, when you transition to cardio, your body must rely more heavily on fat reserves for energy. It’s akin to a hybrid car switching to battery power once the petrol runs low. This metabolic shift helps explain the greater fat loss seen in the weights-first group.

This recent study’s findings align with broader research. A comprehensive systematic review published in 2022 found resistance training alone can significantly reduce body fat and visceral fat, the type linked to chronic diseases. Muscles are metabolically active tissues, continuously burning calories even at rest, which amplifies these effects.

Conversely, performing cardio first might compromise your strength training effectiveness. Cardio uses up glycogen stores, leaving muscles partially depleted before you even lift a weight. It also induces fatigue and may reduce your muscles’ ability to produce explosive power and strength.

A recent systematic review on concurrent training (the practice of combining both resistance and aerobic exercise within the same program) supports this—highlighting that explosive strength gains might diminish if aerobic and strength training occur in the same session, especially if cardio is performed first.

These findings align with other research on concurrent training. A systematic review and meta-analysis examining exercise sequence effects found that resistance-first protocols produced significantly superior strength improvements compared to endurance-first training.

The American Heart Association’s 2023 statement on resistance training confirmed resistance exercise significantly improves lean body mass and reduces fat, especially when combined with other exercise types. However, resistance training alone was found less effective in improving cardiovascular health. This underscores the importance of including cardio in your exercise routine.

source_file: 2025/Citric acid sources .docx
filename: Citric acid sources
answer:
What is citric acid?

Citric acid was first derived from lemon juice by a Swedish researcher in 1784 (1 Trusted Source).

The odorless and colorless compound was produced from lemon juice until the early 1900s, when researchers discovered that it could also be made from the black mold Aspergillus niger, which creates citric acid when it feeds on sugar (1 Trusted Source, 2 Trusted Source).

Because of its acidic, sour-tasting nature, citric acid is predominantly used as a flavoring and preserving agent, especially in soft drinks and candies.

It’s also used to stabilize or preserve medicines and as a disinfectant.

Summary
Citric acid is a compound originally derived from lemon juice. It’s produced today from a specific type of mold and used in a variety of applications.

45k+ 5★ reviews

Natural food sources
Citrus fruits and their juices are the best natural sources of citric acid (3 Trusted Source).

In fact, the word citric originates from the Latin word citrus (2 Trusted Source).

Examples of citrus fruits include:
- lemons
- limes
- oranges
- grapefruits
- tangerines
- pomelos

Other fruits also contain citric acid but in lesser amounts. These include:
- pineapple
- strawberries
- raspberries
- cranberries
- cherries
- tomatoes

Beverages or food products that contain these fruits—such as ketchup in the case of tomatoes—also contain citric acid.

While not naturally occurring, citric acid is also a byproduct of cheese, wine, and sourdough bread production.

The citric acid listed in the ingredients of foods and supplements is manufactured—not what’s naturally found in citrus fruits (4 Trusted Source).

This is because producing this additive from citrus fruits is too expensive, and the demand far exceeds the supply.

Summary
Lemons, limes, and other citrus fruits are the predominant natural sources of citric acid. Other fruits that contain much smaller amounts of it include certain berries, cherries, and tomatoes.

Citric acid is primarily derived from a fermentation process using the mold Aspergillus niger, which produces the acid by feeding on sugars like molasses or corn starch, rather than being extracted directly from citrus fruits, although it naturally occurs in high concentrations in lemons, limes, and other citrus fruits, making them the main natural sources of citric acid.

Key points about citric acid:

Natural source: Primarily found in citrus fruits like lemons and limes.
Commercial production: Most citric acid used commercially is produced through fermentation by the fungus Aspergillus niger.
Process: This mold is fed a sugar source, like molasses or corn starch, to produce citric acid.

My name may make you think of fruit juice, but I’m so much more.
What molecule am I?

Citric acid is an important natural compound that has been known since the late 18th century. The pioneering Swedish–German chemist [NAME] isolated it from lemon juice in 1784. It has since been found in other citrus fruits, pineapples, and even animal tissues.

Citric acid is a major industrial chemical, produced at >2 million t/year worldwide. Its main source is not from fruit, but from the fermentation of crude sugars (e.g., molasses and corn starch) by the mold Aspergillus niger. It has a myriad of uses, mostly in foods and pharmaceuticals; these uses include acidifying agent/pH adjustment, antioxidant, flavoring agent, and as metal salts in dietary supplements. In industry and domestic applications, citric acid is a chelating and buffering agent in many cleaning products and a starting material for synthesizing citrate esters, itaconic acid, acetonedicarboxylic acid, and other compounds.

Biochemists are familiar with the citric acid cycle, which is a major life process in all respiring organisms. Also called the Krebs cycle or the tricarboxylic acid cycle, the process begins with sugar-derived pyruvate, which enzymatically generates acetyl-coenzyme A (CoA) to start the cycle. Acetate released from acetyl-CoA reacts with oxaloacetic acid produced at the end of the previous cycle to form citric acid; this is followed by several steps, during which an oxidation reaction releases energy to the body in the form of adenosine triphosphate.

Many scientists contributed to the discovery and establishment of the citric acid cycle. The two key researchers were [NAME] at the University of Szeged (Hungary) and [NAME] at the University of Sheffield (UK); they were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1937 and 1953, respectively.

Creatine supplementation in youth and adolescence

General rule is ≥18 years unless a younger elite athlete is properly supervised with parent consent.

filename: Curcumin safety and efficacy at the right dosage
answer:
Please give me the scientific consensus on the daily ingestion of 200 mg of curcumin (extract of turmeric), including its safety and efficacy related to general claims such as controlling inflammation, antioxidant functions, antiviral effects, and immune support.

Pro
1 search
20 sources

Current research supports that daily ingestion of 200 mg curcumin is generally considered safe and may offer benefits for inflammation, antioxidant activity, and immune modulation, but its efficacy for antiviral effects and broad immune support is less established.

Safety

Multiple human trials, including those with much higher doses (up to 8,000 mg/day), have found curcumin to be safe with minimal adverse effects, and doses in the range of 200 mg are well below those tested for toxicity. However, curcumin’s poor bioavailability is a known limitation, and co-administration with agents like piperine can enhance absorption.

Anti-Inflammatory Effects

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials show that curcumin supplementation significantly reduces inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). These effects are observed across a range of doses, including those as low as 120 mg, and are most pronounced in individuals with chronic inflammatory conditions. Curcumin modulates key inflammatory signaling pathways, including NF-κB and JAK/STAT, contributing to its anti-inflammatory action.

Antioxidant Functions

Curcumin supplementation has been shown to enhance antioxidant capacity by increasing total antioxidant capacity (TAC) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, and reducing malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, indicating reduced oxidative stress. These effects are consistent across multiple clinical trials and reviews.

Immune Support

Curcumin demonstrates immunomodulatory effects, including balancing Th1/Th2 responses and modulating cytokine production, which may support immune health, particularly in conditions with immune dysregulation. However, evidence for general immune “boosting” in healthy individuals is less robust.

Antiviral Activity

While laboratory studies suggest curcumin has antiviral properties, clinical evidence in humans is limited and inconsistent. Most claims of antiviral efficacy are based on preclinical or in vitro data, not large-scale human trials.

Bioavailability Considerations

Curcumin’s low oral bioavailability limits its clinical efficacy. Formulations with piperine or as metal complexes (e.g., zinc-curcumin) can improve absorption and therapeutic effects.

Conclusion

Daily ingestion of 200 mg curcumin is safe and may help control inflammation and oxidative stress, with some evidence for immune modulation. Antiviral and broad immune support claims are not strongly supported by current clinical evidence. Enhanced formulations may improve efficacy.

Mechanisms

Curcumin inhibits the NF-κB pathway, a central regulator of inflammation, which leads to decreased expression of several proinflammatory cytokines. It also modulates other signaling pathways involved in cytokine production.

Clinical Context

Chronic Inflammatory Conditions: Consistent reductions in IL-1 and TNF-α are most evident in people with underlying inflammatory conditions such as metabolic syndrome or after infection.

Acute Inflammation (e.g., COVID-19): Curcumin supplementation has been shown to reduce cytokine storm markers, including IL-1β and IL-6, in hospitalized patients.

Healthy Individuals: Effects may be less pronounced or inconsistent, especially for IL-6 and IL-8.

Curcumin supplementation consistently reduces IL-1 and TNF-α, with mixed results for IL-6 and little to no effect on IL-8. The anti-inflammatory benefits are most reliable in people with existing inflammatory conditions.

source_file: 2025/David protein bars info.docx
filename: David protein bars info
answer:
Esterified Propoxylated Glycerol (EPG)

Disputed facts

In 2025, the brand David Protein faced scrutiny over its nutrition label after independent lab testing found discrepancies in fat, calorie, and protein content. David Protein disputed the findings, attributing the differences to the use of a modified fat ingredient.

The disputed test results

Fat and calories: A ConsumerLab report cited on Reddit found that a David Fudge Brownie bar contained 9.7 grams of fat and 229 calories, far more than the 2 grams of fat and 150 calories listed on the label.

Protein: A separate test by ConsumerLab found that David bars contained 23.6 grams of protein, falling short of the 28 grams claimed on the packaging. However, this amount was within the 20% margin of error permitted by the FDA.

The company's response

Modified fat: David Protein confirmed that its bars contain a modified saturated fat called EPG. Because the body metabolizes EPG differently—0.7 calories per gram versus the standard 9—the company does not count it toward the fat content on its nutrition label.

Flawed testing: A David food scientist argued that the lab tests were faulty because they used a standard chemical analysis (hydrolysis) that did not account for EPG's unique metabolic properties. The company claimed the testing method "incorrectly identif[ied] EPG as a 9-calorie-per-gram fat," resulting in a factually and legally inaccurate calorie count.

Protein correction: David Protein acknowledged that early batches may have had less protein than advertised but stated that the issue had been fixed. The company also indicated that every current batch is tested to ensure it contains a minimum of 28 grams of protein.

According to published studies, EPG is safe to consume—at least if you don’t binge on it. When three comparison groups consumed 10, 25, and 40 grams of EPG per day, “gastrointestinal adverse events” (gas with discharge, diarrhea, liquid stool…) were reported more frequently by people in the groups that consumed 25 or 40 grams per day, one study found. But 10 grams of EPG per day “was reasonably well tolerated.” David Protein doesn’t disclose how many grams of EPG are in each of its bars. (The company says the 2 grams of fat listed on the label doesn’t include EPG, using the FDA’s classification guidance, but that the ingredient is accounted for in the total calorie count.) David does, however, suggest a limit of two bars per day on its website.

It’s worth noting that the primary studies on EPG were industry-funded, commissioned by EPG’s then owners, and written up years later by [NAME] on behalf of Epogee’s parent company. That the research was paid for by the company that also stood to profit from it might give anyone pause—but like it or not, the arrangement is standard practice in the food world. Both [NAME] and Dr. Davidson insist that their work on EPG went through rigorous FDA review, in part because of the legacy of Olestra. In any case, their studies offer the best available data.

AI Overview

Collagen is a protein that scores 0.0 on the Protein Digestibility Corrected Amino Acid Score (PDCAAS), meaning it is an incomplete protein because it lacks tryptophan, an essential amino acid, and has a low profile of other essential amino acids. The PDCAAS is a method for assessing protein quality, where a higher score (up to 1.0) indicates a higher quality protein. While collagen doesn't contribute much to daily protein requirements, its bioactive peptides offer health benefits for joints, skin, and muscle recovery, especially when combined with other protein sources or resistance training.

What is the PDCAAS?

The PDCAAS measures a protein's quality based on the amount of essential amino acids it contains and how well it's digested and absorbed by the body.

Scores range from 0.0 to 1.0, with 1.0 representing the highest quality protein.

Why does collagen have a low PDCAAS score?

Collagen is an incomplete protein because it lacks the essential amino acid tryptophan.

It also has a lower profile of other essential amino acids compared to other protein sources like meat or whey protein.

What are the implications of this score?

A low PDCAAS means that collagen is not a suitable primary protein source for meeting the body's daily essential amino acid needs.

However, the protein content from collagen does not count towards your daily %DV of protein as it lacks essential amino acids, according to some sources.

Milk protein isolate (MPI) is a concentrated form of milk protein containing at least 90% protein by weight, with minimal fat and carbohydrates, and very little to no lactose. It's made by filtering milk to separate the proteins (whey and casein) from other components, resulting in a powder added to various products like protein bars, drinks, and infant formulas to boost protein content and support muscle growth and overall health.

What "milk protein isolate protein" means:

Isolate:

This term signifies that the protein has been processed to achieve a high level of purity, with most of the fat and lactose removed.

Protein:

It refers to the milk protein itself, which is a complete protein source containing all the essential amino acids.

Key Characteristics of MPI:

High Protein Content: It contains a minimum of 90% protein.

Low Fat and Carbohydrates: The isolation process removes most of the fat and carbs from the milk.

Lactose-Free: It's very low in lactose, making it suitable for many people with lactose intolerance.

Contains Whey and Casein: MPI contains both the fast-acting whey protein and the slow-digesting casein protein, in their natural milk ratio.

Common Uses:

Sports Nutrition: Found in protein powders, bars, and drinks to aid muscle growth and recovery.

Food Products: Used in products like yogurt, ice cream, and soups to increase protein content and improve texture.

Infant Formulas: Its high-quality protein and low lactose content make it a valuable ingredient in some infant formulas.

Who benefits from MPI:

Individuals looking to increase their daily protein intake.

Athletes and bodybuilders aiming to support muscle growth and repair.

People with lactose intolerance who want a dairy-based protein source.

A modified saturated fat known as Esterified Propoxylated Glycerol (EPG) is a fat-like substance created by chemically altering plant-based oils. It contains fatty acids but is modified with propoxy groups, which prevent it from being fully digested, resulting in significantly fewer calories. EPG is used as a versatile fat alternative in foods to replicate the mouthfeel and texture of traditional fats while providing a low-calorie option without digestive side effects.

How EPG is Made

Splitting Oil Components:

The process begins with plant-based oils that are split into glycerol and fatty acids.

Propoxylation:

Glycerol is then reacted with propylene oxide to insert propylene glycol units, creating a modified glycerol molecule.

Esterification:

Finally, the fatty acids are joined to these modified glycerol units, forming the final EPG molecule.

Key Characteristics

Calorie Reduction: EPG delivers up to 92% fewer calories than traditional fats, as only about 8% is absorbed and counted as calories.

Versatility: It is heat-stable, freeze-thaw stable, and compatible with both water and fat-based systems, making it suitable for a wide range of food products.

Sensory Properties: EPG mimics the sensory experience of fat, providing mouthfeel, texture, and a sense of satiety.

Ingredients: EPG is GMO-free, allergen-free, trans-fat-free, gluten-free, and vegan.

Labeling: On food labels, it is often listed as "modified plant-based oil (EPG)".

Common Uses

EPG is used by manufacturers in various foods to reduce calories and saturated fat, including: Protein bars, chocolate and confectionery, ice cream, plant-based meat alternatives, and snacks and baked goods.

source_file: 2025/EAAs and older adults in exercise.docx
filename: EAAs and older adults in exercise
answer:
In the studies below, they did not factor in protein intakes. But that is the overall point. This is free living (i.e., the way people eat), and the EEA supplementation was very helpful. (Also see the Empirical data note below.) For an older person that “thinks” they are getting enough protein from food, at worst, EEA supplementation can guarantee they are (i.e., corrects any math errors). At best, it may improve overall whole-body net protein synthesis for the remainder of a hopefully long life as age-related anabolic resistance increases and overall appetite, including for protein, begins to falter.

Bottom line is that EAA supplementation integrated properly, including in what is known as “protein stacking,” in healthy competitive adults, can help maximize a person’s potential in lifelong whole-body protein synthesis (including muscle protein synthesis), helping most any adult remain active a lifetime. Whether an active adult at 95 yrs of age that has always and still is consuming 1 gm/LB/LBM/protein daily would benefit from using supplementation—who knows or even cares. This person would be an outlier, and I’m willing to guess it would still help, albeit less than the other 99.99999% of the aging population, especially in getting more protein within fewer calories. Further, it would eliminate any math issues. Overall, the preponderance of evidence favors supplementation integration in most all circumstances related to aging and anabolic resistance—there is no need to “cherry pick” data; there is far more in favor, which drives the recommendation.

Here are a few of many well-designed, human studies on essential amino acid supplementation in older adults who exercise, with the key details (who, what, dose, training, outcome), and again, most do not factor in protein intakes, but that is the point:

Randomized & controlled trials (exercise + EAAs)

[NAME] et al., 2012 (J Am Geriatrics Soc)—155 sarcopenic women (≥75 y) randomized to exercise, EAAs (leucine-rich, 3 g twice daily), both, or health education for 3 mo. Exercise + EAA improved knee extension strength (+9.3%) and increased leg muscle mass more than controls; walking speed improved across intervention groups. PubMed

[NAME] et al., 2023 (J Am Nutr Assoc)—Older adults with sarcopenia did supervised resistance training (RT) for 24 wk and were randomized to RT alone vs. post-exercise EAAs (3,000 mg) + tea catechins (540 mg). The RT + EAA (+/- catechins) group gained more skeletal muscle mass than RT alone. PubMed

[NAME] et al., 2019 (J Gerontol A)—Healthy older men & women (non-frail) in a 2×2 RCT for 24 wk: aerobic exercise (AE) ± daily EAAs. AE + EAAs increased muscle strength and EAA-stimulated MPS; lean mass unchanged. Shows function can improve even when mass doesn’t. PMC

EAA trials in older adults (no formal RT, but relevant to muscle)

4) [NAME] et al., 2009 (JCEM)—Healthy older women took EAAs twice daily between meals for 3 mo. Lean body mass increased, and basal MPS and IGF-1 expression rose. PMC

[NAME] et al., 2008 (Clin Nutr)—Glucose-intolerant elderly received EAAs + arginine between meals; lean mass, strength, and physical function improved vs. baseline. (Population was older, not specifically training.) PMC

Mechanistic/acute work in older adults (supports dosing & composition around exercise)

6) [NAME] et al., 2006 (Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab)—In the elderly, EAAs must be leucine-rich to optimally stimulate MPS; higher leucine proportion overcame anabolic resistance. PubMed

[NAME] et al., 2003 (Am J Clin Nutr)—Demonstrated EAAs are the primary driver of amino-acid-induced muscle protein anabolism in the elderly (vs. non-essential AAs). PubMed

[NAME] et al., 2020 (Nutrients)—Leucine-enriched EAA given after acute RT in older adults increased aminoacidemia and mTORC1 signaling vs. placebo, supporting peri-workout EAA use. (Proof-of-concept, signaling outcomes.) PMC

Reviews/position papers that synthesize EAA use in older exercisers

9) [NAME] et al., 2021 (Proc Nutr Soc)—Review concludes leucine-enriched EAA supplements are a practical way to augment per-meal protein and enhance training responses in older adults; often used at ~7.5 g EAA (≈40% leucine) twice daily. PubMed

10) [NAME] et al., 2018 (Br J Nutr) meta-analysis—In mixed older populations with acute/chronic conditions, protein/EAA supplements show variable effects on mass/strength—benefits are more consistent when combined with exercise and in undernourished/frail groups. PubMed

International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: Effects of essential amino acid supplementation on exercise and performance

Anabolic response to essential amino acid plus whey protein composition is greater than whey protein alone in young healthy adults

“Muscle Protein Synthesis and Whole-Body Protein Turnover Responses to Ingesting Essential Amino Acids, Intact Protein, and Protein-Containing Mixed Meals with Considerations for Energy Deficit.”

Essential Amino Acids and Protein Synthesis: Insights into Maximizing the Muscle and Whole-Body Response to Feeding.

Practical takeaways you can use with older clients who train

Dose per serving: Most effective studies used ~3–15 g EAAs per dose; ensure ~2.5–3+ g leucine to overcome anabolic resistance. PubMed+1

Timing: Give immediately post-exercise (or pre), and/or between meals to “top up” suboptimal meals. PMC+1

Who benefits most: Sarcopenic, frail, or lower-protein older adults show clearer gains (mass/strength). Healthy, well-nourished elders may see functional gains without big mass changes unless resistance loading is sufficient. PubMedPMC

Pair with training: Resistance training remains the main driver of hypertrophy; EAAs amplify the training signal and can improve strength/function. PubMed+1

Empirical data from our over 1500 licensed fitness facilities, including college and pro sport teams and the aging competitive athletes we support

Our members (and players) using the ESSENTIAL AMINO ACIDS (EAA) formula, along with normal diet, including meeting protein requirements, continuously comment on better recovery and strength gains, especially the over 60 yr adults. Therefore, the reason we suggest EAA supplementation for much of this population. Further, whole-body net protein synthesis has been shown to improve when combining whole protein and EAA supplementation. A practice most of our college and pro strength, speed, and power athletes (including intermittent athletes), along with others that train like competitors, incorporate into their daily routines—known as protein stacking (multiple protein/amino acid formats). This data has been observed since ~2003, meaning this protocol has survived the test of time and continues to grow.

filename: Age Experience intersect note
answer:
Hi [CUSTOMER],

I will put something together this weekend regarding building your supplement program around training intensity that will give you the best chance of still being able to build muscle naturally.

At some point you will have to come to grips with aging and building muscle. Once you have approached the "age experience" intersection* of training, the only thing you can do is slow the inevitable decline by doing all the right things (e.g., diet, supplements, training, etc.). To continue to add muscle at this intersection, you would have to add hormones, which is not something you want to do because of the future health ramifications. And all you will get is a few more years of building and a very good chance of injury.

*Age experience intersection is a place where the body will naturally plateau in progress and varies for all sports depending on the primary needed function/skill. In other words, physical performance (or size) will no longer improve. As an example: a person competing in tennis (a game of reflexes combined with quickness) most of their lives will reach this intersection in the late 20s or early 30s. A person just starting tennis at age 30 can get better for the next 10 years (so maybe reach the point at age 40–45) but, of course, will never be as good as the professional player who came to their plateau at the other person's starting age.

In the case of weightlifting, if you were a bodybuilder and trained intensely from ages 15 through 40, you will definitely not put on more muscle naturally. But if you started lifting at age 40, you could add muscle for the next few years and then maintain it for many more—but you would never be as big as if you had started in your youth. However, you could be bigger at age 60 than the shrinking bodybuilder by age 60 because of overuse in the latter.

Anyway, that's the "age experience intersection" explanation. Hey, just think, competitive gymnasts come to this point in their teens!

On a personal note, you'll never know the pain I went through after retiring. Watching yourself shrink is tough, but tougher was losing the strength. I just channeled all my passion and thoughts into the businesses, and that took the sting out.

I will send you something soon, my friend.

source_file: 2026/Aging speed measurement -biomarkers to measure age.docx
filename: Aging speed measurement -biomarkers to measure age
answer:
5. I think there's a better way to measure aging for a health/fitness program

For the type of health span/longevity program you're thinking about, I wouldn't rely on one exotic aging test. I'd build a multi-system Aging Score.

Something like:

Metabolic
- HbA1c; fasting glucose; fasting insulin/HOMA-IR; triglycerides; HDL; ApoB
- Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance

Inflammation
- hs-CRP

Organ health
- eGFR/creatinine; ALT/AST/GGT; albumin

Cardiovascular
- resting BP; resting HR; potentially pulse-wave velocity; coronary calcium when clinically appropriate

Body composition
- visceral fat; waist circumference; body-fat %; appendicular lean mass

Physical capacity
- VO₂max; grip strength; lower-body strength; gait speed; balance

Lifestyle/recovery
- sleep duration/quality; physical activity; cardiorespiratory fitness

And then potentially add: DunedinPACE or GrimAge as an interesting molecular layer—not as the final verdict.

That approach is also consistent with the direction aging researchers are moving: aging is multi-system, so composite biomarkers are likely more informative than one clock.

The practical takeaway

If you told me I had to choose between:

A) a $400 epigenetic test saying I'm biologically 58 instead of 65
or
B) knowing my VO₂max, strength, visceral fat, blood pressure, ApoB, HbA1c, insulin sensitivity, CRP, kidney/liver function and muscle mass,

I'd take B without hesitation.

Then I would consider adding Dunedin PACE to B if the goal were to quantify whether a comprehensive longevity intervention appears to be slowing the underlying aging trajectory.

And there is an interesting opportunity here for your Playspan/health-and-performance concept: you could establish a relatively inexpensive “Pace of Aging Score” combining routine labs + body composition + cardiovascular fitness + strength/function and track it every 6–12 months. That would arguably be more useful to a trainer/client than telling someone their theoretical biological age.

Miscellaneous information on speed of aging

Yes. “Speed of aging” can be measured to a degree, and the science is legitimate—but no current test can tell an individual with clinical precision, “you are aging at exactly 0.82× normal.” The field is much better at identifying whether someone appears to be aging faster or slower than peers and predicting future morbidity/mortality risk.

The important distinction is between biological age and pace of aging.

1. Biological age vs. speed of aging

Biological age asks:
“Compared with an average person, how old does this person's biology look?”

So a 65-year-old might have a calculated biological age of 57.

Pace of aging asks a somewhat better question:
“How rapidly is this person's physiology deteriorating right now?”

A pace score might theoretically indicate something like 0.85 biological years per chronological year, versus 1.0 being the population reference. DunedinPACE was specifically developed to estimate this type of rate rather than simply produce an “age.”

2. What biomarkers are actually used?

There are several approaches, and I would divide them into four categories.

| Category | Examples | What it reflects | My view |
|---|---|---|---|
| DNA methylation | DunedinPACE, GrimAge, PhenoAge, Horvath | Epigenetic changes associated with aging/disease/mortality | ★★★★☆ |
| Routine blood chemistry | glucose, HbA1c, CRP, albumin, creatinine, ALP, WBC/lymphocytes | Metabolic, inflammatory and organ-system aging | ★★★★☆ |
| Physical function | VO₂max, grip strength, gait speed, muscle mass, strength | Actual functional aging | ★★★★★ |
| Other molecular markers | proteomics, metabolomics, telomeres, glycan profiles | Different aspects of cellular aging | ★★★☆☆ / emerging |

One well-known clinical-style calculation is Phenotypic Age (PhenoAge). It combines chronological age with routine biomarkers such as albumin, creatinine, glucose, CRP, alkaline phosphatase and several blood-cell measures. These kinds of physiological algorithms have been associated with disease and mortality risk.

3. Epigenetic clocks are probably what you're hearing about

These measure DNA methylation, chemical modifications occurring at specific CpG sites in DNA.

There have been several generations:

First generation
Horvath Clock / Hannum Clock
→ primarily designed to predict chronological age.

Second generation
PhenoAge / GrimAge
→ designed more around health outcomes and mortality.

Third generation
DunedinPACE
→ specifically attempts to measure the rate at which someone is aging.

The newer clocks tend to be considerably more interesting for longevity research than simply asking whether DNA thinks you're 61 instead of 65. NIA reports that newer second- and third-generation measures are associated with functional limitations, cognitive impairment, chronic disease and mortality.

4. Is it legit?

At the population/research level: absolutely.
There is strong evidence that people showing accelerated biological aging on these measures tend to have worse health outcomes. Epigenetic measures can predict disease, disability and mortality beyond chronological age alone.

But there is an important caveat.

At the individual level: we're not quite there yet.
A major recent critique concluded that current epigenetic clocks do not yet meet normal standards for individual clinical decision-making. Different clocks can give different answers; results can be influenced by tissue, laboratory processing, illness, stress and other short-term factors. A change of a year or two in “biological age” after an intervention may even fall within technical/biological noise.

That's a very important distinction when companies advertise things such as:
“Your biological age was 67. After taking our supplement for six months, you're now 59.”

I would be very skeptical of that level of precision.

See #5 at top of document for best measurements

source_file: 2026/Alcohol and cortisol.docx
filename: Alcohol and cortisol
answer:
Yes — alcohol consumption can increase cortisol levels, especially when consumed in moderate-to-high amounts or chronically.

Alcohol acts as a physiological stressor that activates the body’s hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to increased release of cortisol, the primary “stress hormone.” Acute drinking can temporarily elevate cortisol for several hours, while chronic heavy intake may keep cortisol chronically elevated and disrupt its normal daily rhythm. Elevated cortisol from alcohol is associated with impaired recovery, poorer sleep quality, increased abdominal fat storage, muscle protein breakdown, insulin resistance, and negative effects on mood and cognitive function.

For exercisers and athletes, this is one reason excessive alcohol intake can interfere with muscle recovery, body composition goals, performance adaptation, and overall recovery capacity.

Yes — alcohol consumption can increase cortisol levels, especially with higher intake, binge drinking, chronic use, or disrupted sleep caused by alcohol. Cortisol is the body’s primary stress hormone, and alcohol can activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to elevated cortisol both during intoxication and during recovery/withdrawal.

In exercisers and athletes, chronically elevated cortisol from frequent alcohol use may negatively affect recovery, sleep quality, muscle protein synthesis, body composition, mood, and performance adaptation. Even though alcohol may initially feel relaxing, physiologically it often creates a rebound stress response later in the night and into the next day.

Q: There is no protein listed on AminoFormula (AF); can I count it as a protein?

A: You may add 25–40 g (1–2 scoops) of protein to your daily protein intake when using AF as directed, but generally no more, regardless of daily intake. The reason AminoFormula (AF) does not publish a protein amount is because it is purposely not a complete protein, as it contains only the essential amino acids that are directly responsible for protein synthesis activation in proportion to the demand, and therefore serves as a low-calorie, fast-acting, high-anabolic-signaling product for activating muscle protein synthesis (MPS) beyond intact protein itself.

Your total food/shake protein intake throughout the day supplies the remaining amino acids (and they can be made in the body) necessary for the complete and prolonged synthesis. That said, AF can be used to fortify a low-protein meal/food (e.g., plant-based, low-protein breakfast, etc.) to raise the total food protein biological value (BV)—i.e., eliminate the amino acid (AA) limiting factor for MPS indigenous to weaker protein sources. Further, AF is vegan-friendly.

More info:

AF serves to enhance the MPS process beyond protein alone or serve as a low-calorie, high-anabolic extra source of protein. A protein equivalent in 1 scoop of AF is generally counted as approximately 25 g, as it takes approximately 25–35 g of a complete protein to get the amount of the EAA found in one serving of AF, including the 6 g of BCAA. However, regardless of your total AF intake, we advise you only add it as 25–40 g of protein to your 1 g/lb/lean body mass (LBM)/day of protein needs. Mindful that active strength/performance athletes still maintain the 1 g/lb/LBM/day of whole/intact protein sources because different whole-food proteins have other helpful properties/nutrients, including satiety.

filename: ApoB test & results
answer:
What is an Apo B blood test?

An Apo B or Apolipoprotein B-100 test is a blood test that can tell you about your risk for cardiovascular (heart and blood vessel) disease. To do this, it measures the amount of Apo B, which carries substances in your blood that help make plaque, a waxy fat that can block your arteries.

Apolipoprotein B takes lipids where they’re going. But it only gives rides to the kind of lipids that have a bad reputation: low-density lipoprotein (LDL), very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), and others. You won’t find the good cholesterol, high-density lipoproteins (HDL), hanging around with Apo B. When you see Apo B, you can be sure LDL is there, too.

Some healthcare providers believe an Apo B test is more accurate than a lipid panel (which measures all those cholesterol types) to estimate cardiovascular disease risk.

Optimal ApoB Targets by Risk Category

Medical organizations recommend the following targets:

Optimal / Low-Risk: <60 - 80 mg/dL
Moderate Risk: <90 mg/dL
High Risk (e.g., existing heart disease or diabetes): <80 mg/dL
Very High Risk (e.g., recurrent cardiovascular events): <65 mg/dL

Average Ranges by Age and Sex

While "average" isn't necessarily "optimal" for heart health, comparing your score to population percentiles can put your numbers into perspective. Typical population ranges (in mg/dL) include: [1]

Age < 40: 50 - 150 mg/dL
Age 40 - 60: 60 - 160 mg/dL
Age > 60: 70 - 170 mg/dL [1, 2, 3, 4]

Note: The general population average often sits around 100 mg/dL, but modern preventive cardiology considers this too high for ideal, long-term cardiovascular health. [1, 2]

What type of results do you get and what do the results mean?

Your Apolipoprotein B-100 test results can range from 20 to 400 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL).

If your Apo B is higher than 130 mg/dL, you’re at a higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease.

Some cardiology guidelines recommend a target of less than 65 or 80 mg/dL of Apo B. They suggest these goals for people between ages 40 and 75 who take statins.

What is a normal Apo B level?

A normal Apo B level is:
66 to 133 mg/dL for males
60 to 117 mg/dL for females

Conditions that can make your Apo B test results higher

Your Apo B test results may be higher if you have:
A pregnancy.
High cholesterol.
Nephrotic syndrome, a kidney issue.

Apo B testing

An ApoB (Apolipoprotein B-100) blood test measures the number of particles in your blood that carry "bad" cholesterol (LDL). It is considered a more accurate marker for cardiovascular disease risk than a standard LDL-C test, as it directly counts atherogenic particles. High levels indicate increased risk for plaque buildup and cardiovascular disease, often used to monitor treatment.

Key Aspects of the ApoB Test:

Purpose: Measures the main protein found in LDL and other fat-carrying particles.
Significance: Because each LDL particle contains one ApoB molecule, this test directly measures the total count of dangerous particles, better identifying risk when LDL cholesterol seems normal.
When it is used: Recommended for people with diabetes, obesity, high triglycerides, or a family history of heart disease, as well as for monitoring the effectiveness of statin therapy.
